title: Gold, silver imports worth $715 million at Indian Customs, says bullion industry body - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
Consignments of gold and silver imported into India have been withheld at different ports due to delay in update of tariff by the Customs department. While the goods are not being cleared, the Customs department has been charging interest on non-payment of duty, according to the Indian Bullion and Jewellers Association (IBJA).

Imports of gold and silver are being withheld at all Indian ports, as the icegate of DGFT and CBIC-India is not accepting revised tariff rates, said IBJA in an X post on Wednesday.

On the contrary, interest is being charged for non-payment of import duty in clearing the import consignment for no fault on the part of importers, it said, urging the Finance Ministry to rectify the error at the earliest.

The CBIC revises tariff value of bullion every fortnight. The latest revision was effective November 14 with value of gold at $1,245 per 10 g and silver at $1,663 per kg, down from $1,295 and $1,711 on October 31.

Prithviraj Kothari, Managing Director, RiddiSiddhi Bullions, and President, IBJA, told businessline that at the start of FY27, there was delay in DGFT’s annual order naming the banks that are allowed to import bullion.

Even after the list was released on April 17, Customs authorities are yet to issue clearance orders required by port and airport officials, he said.

Customs removed the exemption that banks enjoyed since 2017, and began seeking IGST payments from banks clearing bullion cargoes, he said.

Official sources said the hold-up could possible be due to a technical glitch, which could set right soon.

The issue with silver consignments was more complicated as imports are now “restricted” and even eligible jewellers, importing through India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX), need a valid DGFT Import Authorisation, said Kothari. Every new layer of paperwork adds to the delay before a consignment is released.

As per the industry estimate, over 5 tonnes of gold and about 8 tonnes of silver are stuck at Customs. At Wednesday’s international price of about $3,759 an ounce, 5 tonnes of gold is worth roughly $604 million (about ₹5,650 crore before duty). With the 15 per cent duty included, at the MCX price of about ₹1,30,800/10 g, it is close to ₹6,540 crore ($699 million). This apart, the 8 tonnes of silver adds about ₹115-130 crore ($13-14 million), said Kothari.

In all, the value of metals that could not reach the market adds up to ₹5,750-6,700 crore. The cost was reflected in volume of imports. Imports in April were nearly 15 tonnes against a monthly average of around 60 tonnes during the Akshaya Tritiya buying window, he said.

Most bullion are imported into India on consignment basis. This means the overseas supplier owns the metal until the bank sells it. While it sits at customs, banks pay for vault and storage charges and lose the use of their working capital. If duty is paid late, Section 47(2) of the Customs Act charges interest of 15 per cent a year, said a bullion dealer.

The Government has reduced the export duty drawback rate on gold jewellery by 3 per cent to ₹1,794 per gm (down from ₹1,852 per g). For silver jewellery and specified articles made of silver, the rate has been lowered to ₹26,859 per kg from ₹29,501 per kg. The drawback rates were cut in line with the sharp fall in bullion prices.

The reduced duty drawback rates for gold and silver jewellery exports will lower the refunds available to exporters under a revised schedule notified by the Ministry of Finance.

In July, the duty drawback was increased sharply from ₹773 to ₹1,852 per g to offset higher customs duty of 15 per cent and elevated bullion costs. The rate for silver jewellery and articles made of silver was increased from ₹14,991 to ₹29,501 per kg at the time.
